bet.text: "Touch it, own it": take a piece the moment the robot touches it, bouncing off the substation wall without slowing down.

demand.text: Qualification goals: balance the charge station in auto with the preload and one object, score 3 to 4 links alone, and leave partners room to balance. Playoff goals: preload plus two objects in auto, short cycles, always moving to the next object, and speed to avoid defenders.

auto.text: At the off-season Chezy Champs the team listed autos on both sides and over the bridge. The bump-side auto scores a high cone, a high cube and a mid cube; the bridge auto takes two pieces and balances using the gyro.
A kickstand starts the elevator two-thirds of the way up for a faster first placement.

cycle.text: Slam the double substation with the Laterator in its "springy" mode; the claw's arms latch on and a sensor reports the piece.
The score is a dunk: the elevator drops fast onto the pole and rises again while the rollers run backwards.

endgame.text: Climb last, to fit one more cycle. The Forks swing down beneath partners and raise the robot beside the bridge.

gave_up.text: Sideways cones on the ground were left out as mechanically difficult and, at high levels of play, unnecessary.
Intaking and scoring on one side made autonomous much harder than expected; extra driving time was accepted for a cycle the driver could repeat.
Elevator and Laterator stiffness was a constant struggle and limited how fast it could align and score.

changed.text: The front frame rail kept bending and became solid aluminum, the elevator was stiffened after uprights twisted and welds broke, a ground intake joined a robot first planned without one, and aluminum tubes went inside the Laterator's carbon tubes.
The Articulating Roller Claw replaced the Pinchy Claw after about a month.

outcome.text: 36-5-0 in official play; ranked 7 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 76.04, Archimedes).

solves.text: Drive fast, avoid defense and resist tipping

facts.text: SDS MK4i modules with Falcon 500s for drive and steering
Drive speed
Frame rails and swerve modules are 26 in square, and 1/4 in plates and printed corners make the frame 26.5 in; smaller than usual to save weight and go faster
Two steel bellypans lower the center of gravity; each weighs
A chamfered steel edge plate and wedges over the wheels help it cross the bridge and the bump
Robot weight without battery or bumpers (about 138 lb with them)
Bumpers bolt through the corners of the modules and act as structure

cost.text: The stiff chassis took the bump more violently than teams whose chassis flexed, and the wheel wedges helped only a little with the cable protector

solves.text: Pull cubes from the floor into the Roller Claw instead of letting pieces bounce off it

facts.text: One Falcon 500 drives the roller and another extends the intake by a rack milled into one of two stacked polycarbonate plates
It slides on Teflon and 3D printed blocks instead of bearings, to save weight
The sliding blocks, lined with thin Teflon tape, were inspired by Team 125's early reveal
Roller, extension, gearbox and two Falcons together weigh
The two plates per side are bolted together only at the front and rear, so they flex sideways against a field wall, and a springy software mode lets it stow when hit straight on
The deploy gearbox is held by its own flat sides, the jackshaft and one zip tie, so it lines itself up with the jackshaft bearings

cost.text: In big hits the team thinks the polycarbonate teeth popped over the gear, leaving the rack slightly out of line; it kept working and was reset in the pit in about 30 seconds
The team would cut teeth in both plates, not only the inner one, and extend the block over the mesh, to prevent skipping

functions.name: Articulating Roller Claw

solves.text: Take and firmly hold upright cones and any cubes with one mechanism

cost.text: Complexity and weight were its downsides, both cut down by the time it went on the robot; in cold weather one roller could articulate while the other stayed still, until better springs and warmer weather

functions.type: articulating roller claw for both pieces

facts.text: Arms flip back to make space for a cube, or go over-center to grip a cone at 3 points
Flex wheels center pieces and hold cubes; a Fairlane roller grips cones
Mounted below horizontal by
One Falcon 500 powers the wheels, and a retroreflective sensor triggers when a piece is acquired
It took cones without direct alignment, at almost any height, and at very high speed from the double substation
Inspired by Team 3255's intake

solves.text: Set the height of the Laterator and Forks so the robot can score at every Grid level

cost.text: In testing it twisted easily, some A-frames bent and welds broke
Low-head screws into crush tubes that hold the middle crossbar and the A-frame kept coming loose and cost stiffness; the team does not recommend the joint
The A-frame is smaller than the team wanted: it goes out to the sides because the intake was undecided, and a bumper screw (later removed) stopped it reaching farther forward

facts.text: Full range of motion
Time for full range
One Falcon 500 through a 4.64:1 gearbox
Crossbars and an A-frame stiffen the uprights against twist and impacts
The team says it has no counterbalance and holds at about 16 A all match
Carriage bearings are doubled to spread load into the 1/16 in wall tubes and to strip less powder coat
Most of the stiffening was against sideways sway when the robot turns or stops strafing, a load the team had not designed enough for
An open-ended 9 mm belt is cut to length and tensioned between two milled blocks that grip its teeth

solves.text: Give enough reach and height to score the furthest pieces, and take the hit when the robot slams the substation

cost.text: The team calls it the most iterated subsystem of the season: the practice robot's carbon tubes broke on a peg, and bolt holes, later blamed for many of the breaks, wore and cracked; with aluminum tubes added inside, it still ran when tubes slightly cracked. It suggests no holes, thicker tube and more bushing contact area next time
The team later said the Laterator calculation in its binder, also posted early in the thread, is wrong: it was geared more reasonably, and a corrected sheet was posted

facts.text: Tilted up
Total range of motion
Carbon fiber tubes and plates for stiffness and low weight; PEEK rollers on dowel pins instead of heavier steel bearings
A "springy" mode at the Substation reduces the impact of collisions
Cascade rigged so that all stages extend at once
In the springy mode a low-current hold lets the motor act as a spring; bumpers and claw hit the station wall together so the robot does not tip
Only the first belt has a tensioner; both pulleys of each other stage are on one tube, so their spacing is exact
PEEK bushings lasted all season without lubricant; the carbon tube wore before they did

solves.text: Let the robot hang beside the bridge so the alliance balances quickly

cost.text: They found less use by the championship and Chezy Champs, because most drivers could triple balance fast; they stayed on for Chezy because they did no harm and added rear weight against tipping
The first pocketed side plates bent, so they became solid 1/4 in aluminum

facts.text: Carriage travel
Time for the travel
One Falcon 500 through 14.6:1 pulls Dyneema; surgical tubing raises the carriage to deploy
The rods grew from 1/2 in carbon fiber, which bent a lot, to 5/8 in
Pulling down uses a 1:2 rope rigging, changed from direct pull after the steel bellypans were added
The Falcon in brake mode holds them down for most of the match, balanced against the surgical tubing and gear reduction
At the bottom the fork plates press on the bumper wood and tilt the robot up about 10 deg, to make up for sag

solves.text: Move the Elevator and Laterator together quickly without collisions

facts.text: It generates intermediate states from the current and previous goal, and passes through them faster when less precision is needed
A heading controller snaps the robot to desired directions while driving
Hall effect sensors serve the Elevator and Forks, and one zeroes the Laterator

solves.text: Follow autonomous paths without wheel slip

facts.text: Quintic Hermite splines are optimized for small changes in curvature
Pure Pursuit follows them, with P controllers on translation and rotation error

functions.name: Localization

solves.text: Know the robot's position relative to the nearest AprilTag

functions.type: Limelight AprilTag vision fused with odometry

facts.text: A Limelight at the top of the Elevator is tilted down

A Kalman filter fuses vision with odometry; a pinhole model gives tag distance. The binder has SolvePnP running while disabled; a team reply a week later says SolvePnP was not used and the pinhole model was
Vision was used only for multi-piece autonomous or when drivers had a poor view; as tuned it settled on average more slowly than they did
No vision was used at the first event, Sacramento

functions.name: Battery mount
functions.type: printed connector guide, thin cage and straps

facts.text: A printed ramp speeds battery swaps and holds the connector, with a thumb screw
Two buckle straps do most of the holding, inside a 1/4 in aluminum cage, with grippy tape on the bellypan

cost.text: In an off-season Chezy Champs match a worn strap broke with the thumb screw left out, and the battery unplugged itself

decisions.choice: Slam the feeder station every cycle
decisions.because: the team wanted a consistent, simple cycle the driver could repeat, with no chance of a human player mishandling a dropped cone

decisions.choice: Vertical elevator at the back, then a three-stage Laterator
decisions.because: slamming the station needs an up-and-in pose, and the Laterator's tilt adds height for high cones; a team member adds that it left room to change the intake
decisions.instead_of: an extended arm or angled elevator that has to sneak up on the station
decisions.cost: a long reach: that member would now put the elevator farther forward, for about half the cantilever at the high poses and far more stiffness

decisions.choice: Do not pick up sideways cones from the ground
decisions.because: it is mechanically difficult, and at high levels of play cones are not loose on the ground; big tipped-cone intakes drawn in CAD added complexity and hurt the low center of gravity
it takes cones from a wider area and at different heights, and needs no beam break to capture
decisions.instead_of: the Pinchy Claw, whose thin scoop had durability problems and whose size ruled out a smooth floor intake deploy
decisions.cost: complexity and weight, both cut down by the time it went on the robot

decisions.because: it would have needed a full-width Laterator intake, and the team preferred one that keeps the piece position certain
all stages go out at once, which is faster, and they overlap most at part extension, which is stiffer; with short carbon stages the extra moving mass mattered less
decisions.instead_of: continuous rigging, where stages extend one at a time

decisions.choice: Forks with a more vertical extension
decisions.because: the tall elevator keeps the robot from making the full pivot of low robots
decisions.instead_of: forks that tilt the whole robot up, as on Team 1678

decisions.because: slamming the substation bent thinner rails, which had to be replaced constantly
decisions.cost: weight, placed low at the front

decisions.choice: Two 1/8 in steel bellypans under a pocketed aluminum one
decisions.because: the robot was tippy, and max weight robots were pushing others aside without being much slower; they also stiffened the frame, and the pocketed plate still gives places to zip tie
decisions.cost: about 30 lb, and a fork rigging with more pull

decisions.choice: One Falcon per degree of freedom
decisions.because: the loads were kept low, and speed was limited by stiffness and overshoot, not by the motor; another motor would add over a pound
decisions.instead_of: more motors on the open slots

decisions.choice: Rack-and-pinion floor intake on printed blocks
decisions.because: it was fast to add, light at the tippy front and needs few parts
decisions.cost: a sloppy fit and not the lowest friction, which the team did not mind with two positions and a Falcon
